original: We describe TinySQL-125M, a decoder-only language model for text-to-SQL in which every component of the model path is written from scratch: a byte-level BPE tokenizer, the transformer itself (grouped-query attention, rotary embeddings, SwiGLU, RMSNorm), the optimizer, the training loop, the data pipeline, a grammar-constrained decoder and the evaluation harness. The model is pretrained for about 46 hours on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU on 4.5B tokens of educational web text and SQL code, then fine-tuned on WikiSQL. To make the result interpretable, we fine-tune four public models of similar size (GPT-2 124M, Pythia-160M, SmolLM2-135M and SmolLM2-360M) with an identical recipe, sweep the learning rate for every model, average over three seeds, train our architecture without pretraining as a control, and report confidence intervals and paired significance tests throughout. On the WikiSQL test set, TinySQL reaches 77.95\,$\pm$\,0.18\% execution accuracy with greedy decoding and 80.39\,$\pm$\,0.20\% with schema- and value-constrained decoding (official evaluator: 78.03\% and 80.50\%). This is about one point below GPT-2 and 17 points above Pythia-160M, which was pretrained on 67$\times$ more tokens; SmolLM2-135M, pretrained on 2T tokens (about 440$\times$ more), is 4.6 points ahead. Pretraining accounts for 41 points of accuracy. Constrained decoding never turned one of our model's correct answers into a wrong one in any paired comparison we ran. Small-scale ablations show that rotary embeddings and tied embeddings matter far more than grouped-query attention or an SQL-heavy pretraining mix, and a hand audit suggests that most remaining aggregation errors are label errors in WikiSQL. All code, results and the 166 tests that verify the components are public.

original: Small language models are attractive for text-to-SQL: they run on a CPU, can be deployed next to a database, and are cheap to fine-tune. Most small models available today are pretrained by well-resourced teams on trillions of tokens. This report asks a narrower question: \emph{how far can a single person get on a standard text-to-SQL benchmark with a model whose every part they built themselves, on a pretraining budget of a few billion tokens and one rented GPU?}

original: WikiSQL~\cite{zhong2017seq2sql} pairs 80,654 crowd-written questions with SQL queries over single Wikipedia tables. Its queries select one column, optionally aggregate it, and filter with up to four conjunctive conditions. Strong specialised systems built on large pretrained encoders report test execution accuracy in the high 80s, and their authors attribute a large share of the remaining errors to annotation errors~\cite{hwang2019sqlova}; recent work cleans the dataset for the LLM era~\cite{pihulski2025llmsql}. Multi-table benchmarks such as Spider~\cite{yu2018spider} are harder and are not addressed here.

original: A byte-level BPE~\cite{sennrich2016bpe} tokenizer with 32,768 tokens (256 bytes, 32,500 merges, 12 special tokens such as \texttt{<schema>}, \texttt{<question>} and \texttt{<sql>}). It was trained on 955\,MB of text deliberately weighted towards SQL, plus WikiSQL \emph{training} questions and column names. Common SQL keywords become single tokens (\texttt{\textvisiblespace SELECT}, \texttt{\textvisiblespace FROM}, \texttt{\textvisiblespace WHERE}). Held-out compression is 4.49 bytes/token on FineWeb-Edu and 3.60 bytes/token on the median SQL file. Web, code and forum text is encoded with special tokens disabled, so crawled text containing the literal string \texttt{<sql>} cannot inject a control token.

original: Two facts about WikiSQL motivate it. 95\% of our model's invalid greedy outputs reference a column that does not exist, and 100\% of gold condition values (11,545 of 11,545 on dev) occur verbatim, ignoring case, in the question. We therefore define two levels. \emph{Schema} is a byte-level grammar for the WikiSQL query shape that only admits the table's real column names. \emph{Schema + values} additionally requires every condition value to be a substring of the question (Unicode-aware, valid UTF-8). At each step, candidate tokens are checked best-first and the first that keeps the output a valid prefix is taken, which is equivalent to masking every invalid token and taking the argmax (Figure~\ref{fig:constrained}). The same decoder runs on the baselines through a byte-level adapter for their tokenizers.

original: To find out why, we hand-checked 50 randomly sampled dev questions where our model was wrong \emph{only} in the aggregation. In 31 (62\%; 95\% Wilson CI~\cite{wilson1927} 48--74\%) the gold aggregation is not supported by the question. For example, ``How many people were in the crowd when Essendon was the home team?'' is labelled \texttt{COUNT(Crowd)} rather than the crowd figure, and ``For record 25-24, what is the sum of attendance?'' is labelled \texttt{COUNT}. A further 12 (24\%) are ambiguous, and only 7 (14\%) are clear model errors. Extrapolated, roughly 2 points of dev accuracy are lost to aggregation labels for every model, which is consistent with earlier reports of annotation errors in WikiSQL~\cite{hwang2019sqlova,pihulski2025llmsql}. The audit had a single annotator (the author), not blinded; all 50 judgements are released for re-checking.

original: A single developer can build every component of a text-to-SQL language model, pretrain it on 4.5B tokens in two days on one GPU, and land within about one point of GPT-2 on WikiSQL while outperforming a model pretrained on 67$\times$ more data. Constrained decoding is a cheap and safe addition at this scale. Getting the last points still requires much more pretraining, and on WikiSQL a measurable share of the remaining errors are in the labels rather than in the models.
